transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-09
Time: 10:00 UTC
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Elena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Samira Patel (Redwood CSM); Priya Raman (Quantaco Head of ML), Derek Shaw (Infra), Lina Cho (Product), Aaron Mills (SRE)

Summary:
Quick review of pilot economics: tokens/sec/$ baseline, realized savings from prefix/KV caching, batching tradeoffs for latency vs unit cost; sync on next benchmarks and spreadsheet updates. Agreed to run a larger cache-enabled benchmark and share updated cost model.

Topics:
- Baseline cost/unit econ observed
- Caching (prefix/KV) impact and hit rates
- Batching and tail latency tradeoffs
- Quantization/instance type choices and impact on tokens/sec/$
- Next steps and benchmarking plan

Action items (recap): see metadata list above.

Transcript:
[00:00] Elena (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick check - does the timing still work?
[00:05] Priya: Yeah works for me, hi Elena, hi Marco.
[00:07] Derek: Good morning all.
[00:10] Marco (Redwood SE): Great, so agenda - today we'll focus mostly on cost per token economics and the caching/ batching tradeoffs from last week's runs. I'll share the high-level numbers we got.
[00:18] Lina: Awesome, curious about the real numbers - our execs are asking for tokens per dollar and also the expected savings if we enable prefix cache.
[00:24] Marco: Right, so baseline (no caching, no batching optimization) on the test corpus we saw roughly 3.2 tokens/sec per dollar on the p3-ish equivalent instance, that's for the float16 path. When we enabled quantized INT8 path and some kernel opts it moved to about 5.7 tokens/sec/$ - rough numbers, there is variance.
[00:40] Aaron: sorry can I clarify, tokens/sec per dollar is aggregated across concurrency? how do you normalize?
[00:44] Marco: Good question - we normalize by sustained throughput on a single GPU at peak load with an assumed $X/hour for the instance. For the sheet I used $3.50/hr as the baseline for the underlying GPU equivalent (we note that dedicated pricing/committed capacity changes that math).
[00:58] Priya: and caching numbers? You mentioned prefix/KV caching gave pretty big wins?
[01:02] Marco: Yes - with prefix/kvcache for customer-like traffic (we replayed 50k sessions sample provided by customer), effective tokens/sec/$ increased to about 9.4 tokens/sec/$ in our test when cache hit rate was ~62%. That is mostly from avoiding recomputation for repeated prefixes and saving decoder steps.
[01:20] Priya: 62% hit rate - is that realistic for our app? I thought our sessions had more novelty.
[01:25] Marco (continues): In our telemetry the repeat prefix percent is closer to 40-45% for chat flows.
[01:30] Marco: Right, which is why we asked for your token distribution. If hit rate is 45% then the modeled tokens/sec/$ would be closer to 7.1 tokens/sec/$. The spreadsheet models that sliding scale.
[01:41] Elena: One thing to call out - tokens/sec/$ is sensitive to sequence length distribution. Longer sequences tend to amortize some fixed overheads so per-token costs drop in many cases. Did you see that in the replay?
[01:51] Marco: Yep, in long-form prompts (avg 1k tokens) the tokens/sec/$ on quantized path with caching moved to ~12 tokens/sec/$ at 70% hit, because the fixed KV and key-value load is reused more. For short queries (under 50 tokens) batching and latency become the limiter.
[02:06] Derek: what's the latency impact when you crank batching? We can't blow our 300ms p90 for some routes.
[02:11] Marco: Important point - batch size up to 8 improved throughput but added ~80-120ms to median depending on queueing. For p90 it grew more, so for low-latency routes we recommend small batch sizes (2-4) or auto-adaptive batching by route.
[02:24] Lina: So tradeoffs: if we optimize purely for cost we can push batches higher and use quantized stacks + caching, but that may violate latency SLOs.
[02:31] Samira (CSM): We should map by route: high-frequency low-latency (search/autocomplete) keep hosted low batch, high-cost-sensitivity async routes can push big batches.
[02:40] Priya: Are you using KV cache vs prefix-only cache? what's the difference in your numbers?
[02:44] Marco: We tested both. Prefix-only (simple exact-match reuse) gives modest wins; KV cache - using key-value attention cache across similar prefixes - gives larger wins but requires slightly more memory and warmup. In the run that hit 62% we used prefix+kvcache hybrid. Pure prefix-only at same hit rate gave about 7.9 tokens/sec/$.
[03:03] Aaron: Memory footprint concerns - what GPU memory were you using for these experiments?
[03:06] Marco: Tests were on a 48GB A100 equivalent. Quantized INT8 path reduces memory, so KV cache consumed ~6-10 GB depending on model seq-len. We flagged that in the notes. For smaller GPUs we recommend sharded KV or lower cache TTLs.
[03:21] Priya: Are there any correctness regressions with INT8 quant? we worry about hallucinations raising the false positive rate for our pipeline.
[03:28] Marco: Good callout - we ran a small eval on your prompt set; the quality delta pre/post quantization was within the tolerance you provided in the RBE (you had a 2% delta tolerance). We saw a 1.6% decrement on exact-match metrics and the semantic score was roughly stable. We'll share full eval results in the v2 spreadsheet.
[03:47] Derek: On the costing side, how do you treat cache storage costs and network egress?
[03:51] Elena: We include an estimate for extra memory and storage in the model (small overhead) and an egress/ transfer line for inter-region fallback. But in Dedicated/private models usually network egress is internal. We'll call that out explicitly in v2.
[04:03] Priya: One more on batching - does Redwood support adaptive batching per route? Like route-level SLOs?
[04:09] Marco: Yes - Redwood runtime supports route-level policies. You can set p90 latency targets and have adaptive batching respect them, with fallbacks to smaller batch sizes and higher-cost models for strict SLO routes. We demoed that in the control plane earlier.
[04:21] Lina: For the spreadsheet numbers - can you show us the formula for tokens/sec/$? is it (tokens generated per second) / (dollars per second)?
[04:28] Marco: Exactly. Tokens/sec/$ = throughput tokens/sec divided by $/sec of the instance. In the sheet I normalized $/sec from $/hr. We also show per-call unit economics (average tokens per call * cost/token).
[04:38] Priya: What about caching TTLs - if TTL is too long we might leak private context, any guardrails?
[04:44] Elena: Great security point - TTLs can be route-scoped and we support policy tags. For PII-sensitive routes we suggest disabling caching or encrypting cache keys. Also audit logs are retained and available for review.
[04:57] Aaron: And how does this compare to Anthropic/OpenAI pricing? any quick delta?
[05:00] Elena: In general managed endpoints are sometimes cheaper per-hour but lack the dedicated throughput and local caching options; comparisons in the sheet show Redwood dedicated giving 15-30% better tokens/sec/$ for cache-friendly workloads because of runtime optimizations and batching. But we'll put the explicit comparatives in the v2 cost model.
[05:16] Priya: Ok so immediate asks from us: we'll pull token distribution and target success metrics. We'll look at route SLOs and flag which routes are allowed to use caching.
[05:25] Elena: Perfect. Marco - can you summarize what bench you'll run next?
[05:28] Marco: Sure - I'll run two runs: (A) 5k token replay w/ prefix+KV cache enabled, sampling at 60% and 45% hit rates; (B) batch sweep (1,2,4,8) on the quantized path capturing median/p90/p99 latency and tokens/sec/$. I'll push logs and the raw csvs to the shared drive. Expect results by 2026-09-15.
[05:47] Priya: Sounds good. Also, can you add a row in the sheet for dedicated reserved pricing (committed) vs on-demand? execs care about commit math.
[05:55] Elena: Yep will add committed discount lines and show break-even for 3/6/12 month commits.
[05:59] Derek: One operational note - our infra team wants to know how hot restarts affect cache warmness; if we redeploy instances daily we'd lose some of the benefit.
[06:07] Marco: Right - cache warmup matters. We measured degradation on cold starts - if instances restart, hit rates drop for the first hour; we recommend sticky routing or pre-warming for heavy routes. We'll add a note in the sheet about warmup curves.
[06:20] Lina: Any blockers from Redwood side?
[06:22] Samira: No blockers operationally, just need the telemetry and confirmation on route SLO mapping.
[06:26] Priya: For acceptance criteria - we'll run a 2-week pilot and expect at least 25% reduction in per-call cost for the async routes without increasing error rate beyond 1%. If that meets, we'll talk dedicated sizing.
[06:39] Elena: Good acceptance criteria, we'll record that.
[06:41] Marco: I'll also include a 'sensitivity' tab showing tokens/sec/$ vs hit rate and batch size so you can play with the assumptions.
[06:49] Priya: Great. Thanks everyone - look forward to the v2 sheet.
[06:52] Elena: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the sheet and schedule exec review for 2026-09-18.
[06:58] Derek: Thanks.
[07:00] Meeting end.
